hops.afterHeading: Count each sense by its reliability
hops.title: Two beeps can make one flash look like two
hops.text: It is tempting to think vision always overrules other senses. For location, a sharp visual cue usually wins, as Alais and Burr found. Counting quick events is different. Ladan Shams, Yukiyasu Kamitani and Shinsuke Shimojo paired one flash with two quick beeps, and volunteers often reported two flashes. In a separate timing experiment, one beep started with the flash; the illusion weakened near 70-millisecond offsets yet remained measurable at 115 milliseconds. Shams, Wei Ji Ma and Ulrik Beierholm later compared sound-only and flash-only trials: people counted beeps more reliably than flashes, and combined reports fit a Bayesian model using single-sense reliability and nonuniform flash-beep priors.

sources.citation: Alais D, Burr D (2004). The ventriloquist effect results from near-optimal bimodal integration. Current Biology 14(3):257-262.
Shams L, Kamitani Y, Shimojo S (2002). Visual illusion induced by sound. Cognitive Brain Research 14(1):147-152.
Shams L, Ma WJ, Beierholm U (2005). Sound-induced flash illusion as an optimal percept. NeuroReport 16(17):1923-1927.

hops.afterHeading: A fish that learns to cancel its own pulse
hops.title: A singing cricket turns down its own song
hops.text: A male field cricket faces the electric fish's problem and solves it differently. His ears sit on his forelegs, fully exposed to his own loud song. James Poulet and Berthold Hedwig recorded inside singing crickets, Gryllus bimaculatus. In phase with each sound pulse of every chirp, a signal from the singing circuit weakens transmission at the terminals of the auditory nerve fibers and inhibits an identified auditory interneuron, even in an isolated nervous system singing silently. In 2006 they traced both effects to one identified type of corollary-discharge interneuron. The timed inhibition dampens his response to his own song and helps him stay sensitive to quieter sounds between chirps.

sources.citation: Poulet JFA, Hedwig B (2002). A corollary discharge maintains auditory sensitivity during sound production. Nature 418:872-876.
Poulet JFA, Hedwig B (2006). The cellular basis of a corollary discharge. Science 311:518-522.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A dark field cricket on a blade of grass sings with raised wings while a small pale moth hovers nearby.
image.caption: Brief inhibition dampens a cricket's neural response to its own song, preserving auditory sensitivity to quieter sounds between chirps.

hops.title: The SpeechJammer and the delayed voice
hops.text: In 2012 Kazutaka Kurihara and Koji Tsukada won the Ig Nobel Prize in Acoustics for the SpeechJammer, a gadget meant to quiet people who hog a meeting. A direction-sensitive microphone and speaker play the talker's own words back a few hundred milliseconds late. In a five-person preliminary study, the authors observed the device disrupting speech while a person was talking. Earlier, Yasuki Hashimoto and Kuniyoshi Sakai delayed volunteers' voices by 200 milliseconds in a scanner. Auditory areas in the temporal lobe on both sides were more active than with real-time feedback, especially in people who lost more fluency. The authors linked that activity to monitoring one's own speech.

audio.title: Beeps, crickets and a speech-jamming echo
audio.transcript:
Your brain runs two quiet jobs all day. When two senses report the same event, it decides how much to trust each one. And it can turn down some of the sensory input your own movements produce. Here are three true stories where those jobs show up in odd places.

First, the idea that seeing is believing. When you judge where something is, a sharp visual cue usually wins. Counting quick events is a different job. In two thousand two, Ladan Shams, Yukiyasu Kamitani and Shinsuke Shimojo showed volunteers a single flash of light paired with two quick beeps. People often reported seeing two flashes, even though only one appeared. The authors argued this was a change in what people saw, not just a guess. In a separate timing test, one beep coincided with the flash, and the other could come before or after it. The illusion began weakening at gaps around seventy milliseconds, though it remained measurable at one hundred fifteen milliseconds. A few years later, Shams, Wei Ji Ma and Ulrik Beierholm built a Bayesian model that combined evidence from sight and sound with prior expectations about which numbers of flashes and beeps tend to occur together. People tracked it closely. When the researchers presented sight and sound separately, people counted beeps more reliably than flashes. So when their reports brought the two together, what they heard pulled what they saw toward it. Vision is not the permanent boss.

Second, a creature that has to listen while it sings. A male field cricket has his ears on his forelegs, fully exposed to his own loud calling song. In two thousand two and two thousand six, James Poulet and Berthold Hedwig recorded inside singing crickets and found a tidy solution. In step with each sound pulse of every chirp, a signal from the singing circuit weakens the message passed on by the auditory nerve fibers and inhibits a key auditory neuron. The inhibition keeps its rhythm even in an isolated cricket nervous system that is singing silently, with no sound at all. Both effects trace back to one identified type of corollary discharge neuron. When the researchers mimicked the inhibition, that auditory neuron responded better to the quieter sounds that followed a loud one. The electric fish in this lesson learns a mirror image of its own pulse's sensory effect, and adding that image cancels the predictable part of the input. The cricket takes a blunter route and turns down its response on a timetable.

Third, what happens when your own voice comes back late. In two thousand twelve, Kazutaka Kurihara and Koji Tsukada won the Ig Nobel Prize in Acoustics for a gadget called the SpeechJammer, designed to quiet people who hog a meeting. A direction sensitive microphone picks up a talker's words, and a directional speaker plays them back a few hundred milliseconds late. In a five-person preliminary study, the authors observed speech disruptions that were more common when reading aloud than during spontaneous speech. The echo can make fluent speech falter, and once the person stops talking, there is nothing left for it to disrupt. Years earlier, Yasuki Hashimoto and Kuniyoshi Sakai had delayed volunteers' own voices by two hundred milliseconds inside an f M R I scanner. Areas involved in hearing were more active on both sides of the brain than with real-time feedback, and the increase was larger in people who lost more speech fluency. The researchers linked that activity to monitoring what you say.

So, three stories. When cues go together, the steadier one counts more. Some circuits turn down their own input. And even your own voice can trip you up when you hear it late.
